related_questions.question: How should the minimum wage be raised?
related_questions.snippet: Raising the minimum wage at the federal level requires an act of Congress. Raising the minimum wage in states or localities typically requires state or local legislation or a ballot initiative—and in the case of localities, they may also need the legal power to raise wages above the state floor.

related_questions.question: Is $15 an hour a livable wage?

text_blocks.snippet: No, $15 an hour is not generally considered a livable wage in most of the US, especially in higher cost of living areas. While it might be possible to survive on this wage in certain situations (e.g., sharing expenses, living in a low cost of living area), it often doesn't provide enough income to cover basic needs like housing, food, transportation, healthcare, and other necessities, particularly for families or individuals in high-cost areas.
snippet_highlighted_words: No, $15 an hour is not generally considered a livable wage in most of the US

list.title: Cost of Living Varies:
list.snippet: The cost of living varies significantly by location. In many major cities and expensive states, $15/hour simply isn't enough to cover basic expenses like rent, utilities, groceries, and transportation, especially without roommates or other cost-saving measures.

list.title: Basic Expenses:
list.snippet: A livable wage needs to cover not just basic necessities but also transportation, healthcare, childcare (if applicable), and unexpected expenses, and potentially some savings.

list.title: Impact on Quality of Life:
list.snippet: A low-wage worker earning $15/hour may struggle to afford adequate housing, nutritious food, or necessary healthcare, leading to increased stress and reduced quality of life.

list.title: National vs. Local Standards:
list.snippet: While $15/hour might be closer to a livable wage in some rural or lower-cost areas, it falls short in many urban centers and regions with high living costs.

list.title: Inflation:
list.snippet: The cost of living has increased over time, making $15/hour less adequate now than it was in the past.

text_blocks.snippet: Many organizations and economists suggest that a true living wage is significantly higher than $15/hour, often closer to $20/hour or more, depending on the location and individual circumstances.
